To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the chromatolytic changes of the motor neurones following herpes simplex virus infection are not accompanied by a decrease in the total cell RNA content, that the increased cell volume can explain the decreased cytoplamic basophilia and that the ultrastructural changes are probably secondary to the viral infection.
chromatolysis is associated with a swelling of the cytoplasm and with a disaggregation of polyribosomes.

(1) chromatolytic motorneurones infected with herpes virus contain the same amount of RNA as their normal appearing counterparts; (2) the decreased cytoplamic basophilia of chromatolytic neurone is caused by cellular swelling; and (3) in addition to intranuclear herpes virus particles, a dispersion of ER cisterna and a disaggregation rosettes are found in the chromatolytically altered neurone.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the cytological and cytochemical reactions of neurones following herpes simplex virus infection of the mouse.
the elucidation of the cytological changes in neurones following virus infections.
the study of the cytological and biochemical events which occur in neurones following herpes simplex virus infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the chromatolytic changes observed in the infected motor neurone is not a specific degenerative process but is rather a general response to the virus infection.
chromatolysis is a reaction of neurones to viral invasion, which is characterized by a swelling of the cells, an intranuclear viral proliferation and an increased number of free ribosomes.

the chromatolytic changes observed in neurones infected by herpes simplex virus are due to a combination of the following factors: (i) a cellular swelling; (ii) a dispersion of the ER cisterns; (iii) a disaggregation of ribosome rosette complexes; (iv) an intranuclear infection by herpes simplex virus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the chromatolytic changes are due to the cellular swelling, which is a result of the intranuclear herpes infection.

herpes virus infection of motor neurones leads to chromatolysis, but not to a significant decrease in the RNA content of these cells, and that the virus particles are found in the nucleus and not in the cytoplasm.
the chromatolytic change of the infected neurone is not the result of the loss of the cytoplasmic RNA but rather the result of the swelling of the cell.

we have shown that the RNA content of chromatolytic neurons does not decrease significantly.
